utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Brdjanin. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I hear and I can understand you in a language I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. General Talic, good morning to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. And I can hear you in a language that I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, General Talic. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Andrew Cayley for the Prosecution with case manager Denise Gustin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman. I'm with Tanja Radosavljevic and Milan Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Appearances for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am Natasha Fauveau with Masson Fabien. I represent General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They confused your gender and your name this morning. Yes. Good morning, sir. We are going to continue with your testimony today. And before we do so, I would kindly ask you to repeat the solemn declaration that you made yesterday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Mr. Cayley, when you're ready, you may start.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Cayley. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Simply to inform the prosecutor that I reviewed the statement of the witness yesterday regarding the killing in Kraljevica. As far as I understand, that statement contains information that we do not accept, and I would like the witness to appear. If nevertheless the Prosecutor wishes to tender the statement through 92 bis, I would request that the witness be present for the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, I know that this is more -- is it your compartment or is it Ms. Korner's?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I can deal with this, Your Honour. We'll call the witness. We'll call the witness. But it does mean -- I'll deal with the order of witnesses at the end, because that witness, 7.76, was actually the third witness in the list after this witness. But now we're going to have to rearrange the list. But I'll give you the definitive list at the end of today's session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If necessary, since -- anyway, we'll come to that when we come to it. So the witness will be brought over.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed with your examination of the witness, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Examined by Mr. Cayley: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, let me just remind you where we left off yesterday. We had reached the 19th of April of 1992, and you had just started to speak about the ultimatum that you had received from Mr. Rasula. Could you tell the Judges of the events as you remember them of what happened in the municipal building after you received that ultimatum and what you did.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 19th of April, 1992, somewhere approximately 9.30 p.m., Rasula called Suad Sabic and said that he is setting an ultimatum and that by 22 hours we go out of the building and go into the park, lay down the arms, hand ourselves over, and that nothing will happen to us. But if we don't do that, we -- the building of the municipality will be attacked. We accepted the ultimatum to think over what our options are. We were on the windows -- looking through the windows, and through the windows we could see the movement on the right side of the building. And he said from the direction of Djedovaca a bigger column of cars is coming. We knew that that was Colonel Basara from Lusci Palanka with the 6th Krajina Brigade, which was stationed there. At that point we agreed to exit from the side exit door, and most of us left for the village of Sehovci the nearest village to Sanski Most, and a smaller group left for Gornja Mahala, upper Mahala.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 757.2, which is the map of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But while that is being taken care of, let me ask you a question. You said in your evidence "and he said from the direction of Djedovaca, a bigger column of cars is coming." Who said that a column of cars was coming from Djedovaca?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: A -- a person who was looking through the window and could see this column of vehicles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could put the map of the projector next to you. Now, did you yourself see this column of vehicles?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were in Sanski Most. Can you show the direction from where this column of vehicles was coming from.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The column of vehicles was coming from the direction of Lusci Palanka. So it's -- along the normal road would be Lusci Palanka, Miljevci, Gorica, Naprelj, Kamengrad, Donji Kamengrad, Podbrijezje. Meanwhile this column was coming from the opposite direction, from Lusci Palanka to Jelasinovci, Stanici, Djedovaca, Sanski Most. The map doesn't show this road. Lusci Palanka to Jelasinovci, Gonji Dabar and Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At what point on that route were you able to observe these vehicles?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could notice the column of vehicles maybe some five minutes after receiving the ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whereabouts was the column of vehicles when you saw it? How far away from Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: This column was at a distance of some 2 kilometres from Sanski Most. That's the hill -- a hill, and they were descending the hill towards the valley of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the column was 2.000 metres away from where you were observing it from; correct? Approximately.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How high from the ground were you when you were observing this column?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was on the first -- standing on the first floor of the municipal building. So there's the ground floor and the first floor of the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you say that you knew it was the 6th Brigade. Why did you and others conclude that the column of vehicles was the 6th Brigade coming to Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, such a big column couldn't be anything else but a column of the army, the column of the 6th Krajina Brigade. And we assumed, and 99 per cent were convinced, that it go -- that it was going around this other route, Dabar, Celavica [phoen] and a round about way to then Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you stated in your evidence that you eventually withdrew from the building to Sehovci. Do you know what happened at the municipal building after you left?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: After we left -- it was somewhere around 10.00 p.m., 22 hours. We could hear shell fire and explosions, because also the village of Sehovci are some 2 to 3 kilometres from Sanski Most. Also in the village of Podlug, which are vis-a-vis the village of Sehovci, we could hear there were bursts of gunfire, shooting, explosions, and also vulgar songs at the expense of Bosniaks and Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could just point on the map to the village of Sehovci, just to show its proximity to Sanski Most. If you can see it there.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: And Podlug is here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I know subsequently you had sight of the municipal building. And we'll come to that in a moment. I'd like to move to the next day, the 20th of April of 1992. What happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: After arriving to Sehovci, we spent the night there and somewhere, at about 7.00 a.m., five past 7.00, Rasula called us. More concretely, he called Redzo Kurbegovic. And he said that we should come for talks to the municipal building in Sanski Most exactly at noon, that also General Talic would be coming.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go to that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, we did go. But I wanted to say that we refused this invitation because he said he would be coming and that their police would be escorting us. We said we wouldn't go if we will not be escorted by our legally appointed police as our escorts. And we then didn't come to an agreement. And then exactly at 8.00 p.m. -- 8.00 a.m., Rasula called again. He said he agreed that we come accompanied and escorted by our police, the regular police. We accepted this, and we went and attended that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be giving Prosecutor's Exhibit 759, please, which is, Your Honours, Rasula's diary. Mr. Usher, I'll need to find the page from this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, this is the diary that we looked at yesterday. I'm aware that you don't recognise the handwriting, but this diary gives an account of a meeting at apparently which you were present. So I want to go through the entries of the diary and then I want to ask you what you remember from your memory of what happened that day. Now, do you recall where the meeting was held?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was held in the building of the municipality, in the room -- the premises of the chief, Rasula.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's on page 15 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the meeting indicates that those present were General Talic, Colonel Basara, Major Zeljaja and representatives of the SDS, SDA, and HDZ. Now, on the next line it states present, Mirzet, Redzo, Sabic, Ante, and Vlado. Now, who is the Mirzet referred to there?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It refers to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Redzo?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the SDA party, Kurbegovic Redzo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Kurbelovic or Kurbegovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kurbegovic Redzo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sabic?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Suad Sabic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ante?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ante -- I cannot remember the surname. Oh, it's Tunjic. Tunjic Ante.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the last one, Vlado, do you remember who that was?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must have been Vlado Vrkes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next line then reads -- and I'm not going to go through all of it, because it's not, I know for you, very easy to read. But in particular, what I want to go to is the -- where it states "demand." And that is on page 16, Your Honours. "Items. 1: Guarantee of the public safety of citizens and their property. "2: The establishment of the organisation and functioning of the legal public security service and police station by finding the appropriate facilities and dividing resources. Deadline, immediately. "3: The functioning of the legitimate municipal assembly and its organs. Deadline, immediately." I'm not going to read 4. It's dealing with the economy. "5: The establishment of activity by all public institutions and company -- and companies with special emphasis on the work of the radio station with parity programming. Deadline, immediately. "6: The determination of the sequence of events on 18 and 19 April, 1992 through the work of a mixed committee with the presence of European Community observers and representatives of the regular army. "Objection. A, against the military police. Mostly from Prijedor without having criminal individuals involved, Jovic [phoen], Lukac. B, Colonel Basara's driver irritates them." Now, Witness, those demands, are they broadly what you remember the demands being at that meeting on the 20th of April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember anything else that was demanded, apart from these matters referred to here?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was the demand that General Talic directly goes to the radio station of Sanski Most and to present the conclusions, so that the public would be informed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll come to that in a moment. Do you remember any discussion of checkpoints at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they were discussed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did the representatives of the SDA demand in respect of checkpoints, if anything?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that the checkpoints be withdrawn and that the -- also the army be withdrawn from the checkpoints. And this was one of the first items on the conclusion side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was -- were the activities of the 6th Brigade discussed at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what activities were discussed specifically of the 6th Brigade with General Talic?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, that the checkpoints be removed, disbanded, and that the shooting stop so that it won't be -- there would be no more intimidation of the population, that there be no drinking bouts, no more drinking bouts. And these were the main items.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anything discussed about the numerous explosions that had been taking place in Sanski Most during the past few months?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Also that the explosions should stop, as up till then we had 42 explosions. And normally -- and this was being carried out by the legitimate bodies of law and order to detect who the perpetrators were and that they be brought to justice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And here you're talking about the perpetrators of the explosions within Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's now move on through Rasula's diary. And you are quoted in it. And again, this is not a transcript. This is a summary of somebody else's understanding of what was said at the meeting. But I'm going to read out apparently an abbreviated version of what you said. "Mirzet: The result of cooperation is last night's success. We received a telex from the Territorial Defence about its mobilisation, but we were in the process of reaching agreement. Ignored the national structure percentages. The SDS party is taking the SUP building and the president says you have no place here any longer. "Moving into the building as a temporary solution, we have accepted everything that was rested from us, but we are still being given new demands. Let us divide ourselves to the least possible extent and what about our workers in Rudnik Famos. The question of the army, but who is in it? The SDS can do nothing to the military police." Now, I know again we're talking about events that took place ten years ago -- over ten years ago. Do you remember speaking of any of those matters in that meeting on the 20th of April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just one matter that arises. I mentioned to you a moment ago that it was stated that Colonel Basara's driver irritates them. Now, is that the Colonel Basara's driver that put a gun to your head in the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Macola.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let us go to the final part of the meeting and General Talic's apparent comments, concluding remarks. And I'll read it to you and then I'll ask you specifically what you remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's simply for the record that this part -- we'd like to know which part Mr. Cayley is referring to now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have the B/C/S version in front of you or the English, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the B/C/S version, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Cayley, perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to my cross-examination of the previous witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's the final part of the --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. There seems to be a serious problem with the interpretation. What I wanted to say is that we contest the authenticity of this part of Rasula's diary -- alleged Rasula's diary. And I am relying on the cross-examination that I had with the previous witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Well, I mean, I can make no comment. She'll bring a handwriting expert to say that just that piece is being forged or something. We'll wait and see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, in other words, you're not querying the part of this diary alleged to originate from Rasula? You know which part he's putting his question from. No? One moment. What's the problem, general? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] I contest the entire diary as the accused. It's inaccurate. It's incorrect. And what the Prosecutor is quoting was never mentioned. That was never mentioned at the meeting, the question of the United Nations and things like that. I was present at that meeting, and it is not mentioned anywhere in the witness statement. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's okay. THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Please forgive me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have every right if you want to put an interjection somewhere, provided you do not make statements or take over, instead of your lawyer, you have every right. I think we -- more or less we know where we are. I mean, initially I thought you wanted a clarification from Mr. Cayley as to the relevant part of the alleged diary of Mr. Rasula where he was referring -- where he was referring to, to which the question referred. But I understand that's not your problem. Your problem is that you -- you wanted to put for the record that you are contesting this particular part of the diary. And now as General Talic puts it, the entire diary. This is the situation as I see it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may clarify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, general. You may sit down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This part of the diary is clearly forged. On the other hand, it is quite clear that if a part of a diary, one doubts seriously that a part of the diary has been forged, then one doubts the authenticity of the entire diary. So we contest it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Am I on the record --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: To whole diary is challenged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how I take it. That's how I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just read --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It doesn't stop you from putting questions, obviously. I mean, it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No. It's for the Defence and General Talic to bring evidence to suggest it is a forgery, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But do inform -- because I think you ought to tie up with Ms. Korner on this, because she was here conducting the testimony of --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I read that section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me read to you, Witness, what apparently General Talic said. And I'll read the -- I think it's six or seven lines. "General Talic, concluding remarks. Reach agreement but without undue delay. The police added -- military police from Prijedor shall remain and if need be from Banja Luka. We do not recognise the paramilitary formations. We are not allowing barricades to be put up. The JNA, Yugoslav People's Army, will guarantee the peace of the citizenry and the security of property. We are asking for your help. Added, otherwise you will see/ "see" crossed out/ don't call anyone for help otherwise you will have Kupres, Bosanski Brod, Vukovar. The Banja Luka Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Mufti has appealed for peace. Listen to him."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think Ms. Fauveau has an interjection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry. I was trying to -- Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apparently there really is a serious problem with this part of Rasula's diary, because the previous witness -- the text of what is written here -- [In English] "Do not ask for the help." [Interpretation] Now, Mr. Cayley says that in this part of the diary it says we are asking for your help and previously it said we are not asking for your help.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No. In the English translation it actually says both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. I think it -- I understand what you mean, Madam Fauveau. But I think what's important for the time being for us to be able to follow is what is contained in this bottom line and a half on page 17 of the alleged diary. And that way we can leave it at that. I mean, I know what the previous witness said. I suppose Mr. Cayley knows too, from what I gather. So I think you can -- you may proceed with the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Shall we find out what this witness has to say?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Karabeg, you've heard those concluding remarks, and you've also heard all of the objections being raised. From your recollection, from your memory of ten years ago, what do you remember being said by General Talic?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me see. These words from the diary were spoken by General Talic in that context, because the agreement was that we get together in the municipal building alone at 6.00 p.m. after he left. And I remember that we were saying goodbye. We shook hands. And when I shook hands with Colonel Hasetic, he held my hand tightly. I felt that this had a meaning to it, but I made no comment. But after they had left, me, Suad, and Redzo got together and I said, "Redjo and Suad, did Colonel Hasetic grip your hand firmly?" And they said yes. And this was a sign as if to let us know that we should take care. And General Talic was threatening, mentioning Kupres, Vukovar, something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is your best recollection of what was said on that day.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did General Talic subsequently go on to the radio and announce the demands that apparently had been agreed?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we requested that these conclusions be announced on the radio, the director of Radio Sana, Mr. Orlovic, said that was unfeasible, and General Talic said that he was in a hurry, and we said, "Well, that's simple. Pick up the telephone and the general could make the announcement live over the telephone," so that it wasn't announced over the radio.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the agreement was to get together again at the municipal building at 6.00 p.m. That evening; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All of us - General Talic with his associates left for Banja Luka. And we as representatives from all the parties from the territory of Sanski Most municipality were supposed to meet in the municipal building at 6.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you in fact meet in the municipal building at 6.00 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went there, and I found the iron hedgehogs in front of the building, and the police there -- obstacles, in fact. And I was told, "What kind of a meeting? Who told you about it?" So no meeting was held.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after that meeting, were the checkpoints removed from around the town?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The situation worsened that very evening, that very day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did it worsen?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation got worse. First of all, in respect of increased intimidation, shooting into the air, bursts of fire into the air, we also saw larger numbers of army members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about explosions in and around Sanski Most? Was there a decrease or an increase?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you. I can't say for that particular evening, but now the explosions occurred every four or five days, not every 15 or 20 days. Now they occurred every four or five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 622, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this is a regular combat report from 5th Corps command from General Talic's command. It is signed on behalf of General Talic. The paragraph that interests me is paragraph 3. And the relevant part -- this is the second paragraph, Your Honours. "The situation in the areas where excesses occurred is now under control, and the visit of the Corps Commander to Sanski Most and his tour today of Babanovci have had a calming effect on the situation." Now, you were in Sanski Most during these days. In your view, did General Talic's visit to Sanski Most have a calming effect on the situation?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had the opposite effect. The least of all was it a calming effect. The situation became worse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, subsequent to your meeting with General Talic, did you have any more communications with him after the 20th of April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I forgot to mention that on the 20th of April, as we parted General Talic addressed me as the representative of the civilian authorities and said, "President -- Mr. President, if the situation gets worse, here is my telephone number. Please feel free to call me." And I noted down his telephone number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you call him?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't call him on Tuesday, that is, the next day, because I thought that the people from the SDS would do as they were told. But as the meeting didn't take place at 6.00 p.m. when it was scheduled, I thought that probably they would call us the next day. This didn't happen. And then on the 27th -- actually, on Wednesday I dialed General Talic's telephone number. I was surprised and was glad that within 15 or 20 minutes I was managed to reach him. That is, they connected him to me. I managed to get in touch with him. We talked. The first thing I said was that the scheduled meeting for 6.00 p.m. had not been held, that Rasula did not schedule another meeting, and that the situation in Sanski Most was worsening. His response was -- he swore at them -- he swore at Rasula, that he's cheeky, that he's impudent, that he's an extremist. And hearing that, I was glad. He sounded honest and sincere to me. However, the next day, as I was watching the daily news programme on television, I think there was a short clip from the previous night, a celebration in Banja Luka. I saw General Talic with all of these others, Karadzic, Krajisnik, Plavsic cordially greeting each other, hugging each other. And then in the large group I also noticed Rasula. And then I thought to myself well, this man is really lying to us. He's misleading us. They're saying one thing and doing another. And after that, I never saw him or heard him again until yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After your contact with General Talic, did you have any more contact with Colonel Basara?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges about your contacts with Colonel Basara. And before you answer that question, was it your understanding that Colonel Basara was the subordinate of General Talic? And if you don't know, just simply say, "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: He should have been, because at the meeting that we attended one could see that Colonel Basara was subordinate to General Talic, when we were in the municipal building on the 20th of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, again, if I could repeat my question: Can you tell the Judges about your contacts with Colonel Basara after the 20th of April of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. You see, we had several meetings with Colonel Basara because he was our only hope and our only way of communicating with the SDS, though they refused any contact persistently. The same occurred with Colonel Basara. We even came out with a proposal, or specifically Fuad Kurbegovic did, on behalf of the League of Communists, that Basara be proclaimed honorary citizen of Sanski Most municipality. He made a lot of promises. He promised that he would keep the army under control, that there would be no searches at the checkpoints, that there would be no drinking bouts, that there would be no bursts of fire. And in fact, the opposite occurred: The number of checkpoints increased; there were machine-gun nests set up; two APCs in the municipality; and it all came to a head with an explosion one day. Actually, there was an explosion every night, so it wasn't every three or four nights but every night now. So the situation became worse and worse. It went from bad to worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 626, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, this is a conclusion of the meeting of the Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most held on 28 April. And the gist of it -- I'll read paragraph -- I won't read all of it. "All citizens in the area of Sanski Most municipality who possess any kind of weapon shall hand it in to the public security station, the closest unit of the Yugoslav People's Army, or the staff of the Territorial Defence of the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most." And then it gives times for the handing in of weapons, and then it says: "Citizens who have private weapons with a licence from a competent organ and members of armed Territorial Defence formations, active service and reserve police and the Yugoslav People's Army are exempt from this decision." Were you aware of this decision at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that the population was being disarmed at the end of April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were all ethnic groups within the population being disarmed as far as you remember? Were Serbs, Croats, and Muslims being disarmed at this time?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only the non-Serbs were being disarmed. Only those people who were not Serbs. That means Bosniaks and Croats and others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know this?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know because that is what was being done, and I saw it with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the last paragraph of this document states that: "The Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most meet with the commander of the 6th Krajina Brigade, Colonel Basara, and start regulating the relationship between the armed forces of the Serbian Territorial Defence and the Yugoslav army." Did you know at this time, at the time that you were meeting with Colonel Basara, that he was also meeting with the Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you still have Rasula's diary?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Does he still have 759? This, Your Honours, is on page 37 of the English translation, and it is a meeting of the Crisis Staff on the 24th of May of 1992. That's how it is represented.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'll read it to you, Witness, if it's not possible for you to read it. "Item 3: The operation was successful. So far only in the case of weapons belonging to the Territorial -- Territorial Defence and the republican police, while nothing has been done about weapons from illegal sources." Witness, is that referring to the disarmament process that was taking place at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next line reads: "Colonel Basara proposed a strike at the strongest point. Colonel Anicic suggested Bojancic [phoen], Demasevici [phoen], Vrci, and Okrec [phoen]. The next line, this is on page 38, Your Honours. "Colonel Basara will prepare an operation against Dimitrovici [phoen]" -- next word is illegible. "The proposal was not accepted. It was decided that it should take place on Tuesday morning." Now, Witness, if this was -- this meeting was held on the 24th of May of 1992, which was a Sunday, would you agree that the following Tuesday, certainly by my calendar, must have been the 26th of May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was Anicic, Colonel Anicic? Do you know who that was?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met Colonel Anicic. I don't know him too well. He was born in Sanski Most -- the municipality of Sanski Most, but he served out of Sanski Most. So I knew him superficially.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what his function was at this time within Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, at the time and in those contacts, I had no contact with him. But as far as I was informed and as far as we knew, he headed the Crisis Staff of the municipality of -- that is, the Serbian municipality of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever meet with him?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I hadn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not he was in the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, he was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you know.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 638.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I don't want you to read all of this document, but if I could just direct you to the stamp and signature at the top where it states, "approved by Serbian Territorial Defence commander Colonel Nedeljko Anicic." And then by the side of that it states, "Strictly confidential. Grmec 92." Now, I just want to read a couple sections of this combat order. And I'll ask you some questions in a moment. Paragraph 3 of the order, and the subject matter of the order is disarmament operation in Sanski Most. Paragraph 3: "The 6th Brigade in coordinated action with the STO units -- Serbian Territorial Defence units -- is undertaking combat operations in Sanski Most municipality area in order to disarm enemy forces by placing its main forces on the Skuceni Vakuf, Kamengrad-Dolina valley. Sanski Most Vrhpolje access with emphasis on the general sector of Sanski Most." Over the page on page 2 of the English version, Your Honours. And this is in your version, Witness, is paragraph 4, where it reads, "I have decided." And then in the next paragraph, it states: "Once the positions have been taken, use Serbian Territorial Defence units to prevent the insertion and operation of sabotage groups in the Serbian villages. After artillery preparations, disarm the settlements of Mahala, Otoke, Muhici, Marije Bursac the Omladinsko neighbourhood, Alagica neighbourhood. In coordination with the 6th Brigade units, in order to cause the enemy great human, materiel, and technical losses." And then in the next paragraph: "Engage the main forces for tasks in the Sanski Most sector. Re-subordinate the sector staffs along with the Dabar, Lusci Palanka, Budimlic Japra units and the Koprivna, Ostra Luka and Usorci Territorial Defence units to the 6th Brigade command for operations along the secondary axis of attack." Paragraph 9, the second sentence. This is the part, Your Honours, dealing with artillery preparations for the operation. "Upon completion of artillery preparations with the remodelled Georgi vehicle and in coordination with armoured combat vehicle from the 6th Brigade, it will neutralise the remaining fire targets and search the Mahala sector further towards the Ekonomija." And then the order goes on to essentially task them for intervention on separate orders once this order is complete. Do you see the section at the bottom, Witness, that states "deliver reports on" -- it's on the last page, on page 5. It's on the final page. Do you see that? It says "deliver reports on," and then colon, "readiness for the attack at 0500 hours on the 26th of May." Do you see that, Witness?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. I see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall a moment ago I read out to you from Rasula's diary that the attack was postponed until the 26th of May, that Colonel Basara's suggested attack was postponed by them until the 26th of May? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I remember it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you still have Rasula's diary with you?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Is it in front of the witness? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you can -- I don't know if you'll be able to find it. But the part that deals -- it's actually the next day, the 25th of May of 1992. And I can read this out to you, because there's not very much in there that I want to direct you to.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But this, Your Honours, again is on page 38 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's headed, again, "Crisis Staff, 25 May 1992." "1: Information on security of important features." "2: Report on the developments in the municipality over the past 24 hours." "3: The disarmament plan and its beginning." "4: Preempting enemy operations. A, arrest of leaders. B, detention facilities. Miladin Papic and Mico Krunic." "Item 4: Take into custody Adil Draganovic in Mahala." 30 pieces were returned -- that he failed to turn in, arrest Redzo Kurbegovic, Mirzet Karabeg. And then there's a whole list of names that I won't read out. "Item 3, Tuesday at 6.00 or 7.00 the operation begins. The fighting will not stop until they surrender. Take no prisoners if armed. Captured civilians to be used for exchanges." Mr. Karabeg, what happened to you on the 25th of May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, I was arrested, and I was taken to the headquarters of the police station. Two vehicles came with eight armed individuals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whereabouts were you taken?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was taken to the police station and precisely to the detention facility in the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I just have a set of photographs, Your Honours, which I'd like to show to the witness. Can you give copies to the Defence and to the Judges, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise this building, Witness?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is this building?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: This building is the police building in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is this where you were taken on the 25th of May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you taken in the police station?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The prison facility there, which is located behind this building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the prison facility can't be seen in this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, it cannot be seen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And whereabouts within the prison facility were you taken?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was cell number 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was in the cell with you?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found two people already in this cell, Ibro Kuzelj, Katkic Meho, a retarded person, Atlija Marinko, and in the next cell I heard that Ismet Jakupovic was there, Ismet Alagic, Stipe Catic, Adil Draganovic, and Fikret Saletovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that one of the people that was in the prison with you was a retarded person. What was he doing in the prison with you?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even I personally really don't know. But -- because he wasn't a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he subsequently released?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was. The next day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to you on the day that you were taken to your prison cell on the 25th of May, if anything at all worthy of note?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say I was taken there in the hall. A policeman took me over. He took my belongings, my wallet, my belt, shoelaces from the shoes, and then he took me to the cell number 2. Nobody hit me and nobody mistreated me. Nobody beat me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened the next day, on the 26th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the next day, the 26th of May, 1992, we received visits from the SDS, Boro Savanovic, Papric Miladin, and Tripkovic Nemanja. They talked to us, and I told them, "Well, okay if you arrested us, but why -- what's wrong -- what wrong did this man commit? He knows nothing. He's retarded. It would be proper if you let him go." And in fact, on that day in the afternoon he was freed and they let him go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And his name again, the man that was retarded?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Meho Katkic, also known as Znojko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Here I'm getting confused. Before, when he first referred to -- in answering your question who was in the cell with you, he said -- I found two people already in the cell, Ibro Kuzelj, a retarded person, and Atlija Marinko. And in the next cell I heard that -- et cetera, et cetera. We're not interested in those.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think it was a generic description of a person without a name, Your Honour. That's why I was asking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But that would make it three -- or four and not two persons in the cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'll clarify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived, Mr. Karabeg, how many people were in cell number 2 and what were their names?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three people. Ibro Kuzelj, Katkic Meho, also known as Znojko, a sick, retarded person, and Atlija Marinko, as well as then I joined them as the fourth.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Your Honour, we're going to -- there's going to be a lot of this people in cells, who they were. I mean let's face it. It's ten years ago. I don't remember who I was in two weeks Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. It's not important, Mr. Cayley. What's important is I did get the impression initially when he was answering your first question that although we were being told that he was saying two persons, in actual fact I did understand that there were -- there were more than two -- there were more than two persons. So now it's clarified and you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did Mr. Papric say anything on this occasion, on the 26th of May?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I will return to the previous question. But let me tell you, in that cell we spent -- seven of us spent the night, because after that some other people were also placed in the same cell. Now a concrete answer to your question, yes, Miladin Papric turned to Redzo, who came to -- was placed in a cell, and he said, "There you see, Redzo, what you wanted to do was get national -- a party of your own, and look -- look what happened." And so this is what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you are referring to Redzo, are you referring to Redzo Kurbegovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Redzo Kurbegovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've not mentioned him as being in your cell at the police station. Where did Papric speak to Redzo?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was talking in cell number 2, but he was brought -- he spent the night with me in that cell but he -- and he was brought in later in the evening, on the 25th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let's make this absolutely clear. On the night of the 25th of May, what was the total number of people that were in the prison cell with you?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seven.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So not including the three that you've already mentioned, who were the other four that were brought in?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have mentioned the three who were there already before me. Myself, the fifth was one Haso Osmancevic, Nedzad Muhic, the sixth person, and Redzo Kurbegovic was the seventh person to be placed in that cell that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Is that clear to Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was on the 26th, the next day, that Papric had the conversation with Kurbegovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, who, if you know, was in charge of the prison at the SUP station?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The head of the police station for the -- Vujanic Drago and Krunic Mico, they were responsible for the prison facility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at this time on the 25th, 26th of May, 1992, who was in charge of the police in Sanski Most, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. May I correct myself?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have -- I mixed up the police station and the prison facility with the camps, and that is why I have mentioned these two persons, Mico Krunic and Drago Vujanic. For the police, there was the police chief who was the responsible person in authority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was his name, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vrucinic Mirko was the head of the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And because I don't fully understand what you've said. Who did you understand to be in charge of prison facilities at the SUP on the 25th and the 26th of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Papric. Papric Miladin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when he ceased to be the commander of the prisons? Was he ever replaced? If you don't know, simply say "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, this was chief of police who was already retired. And on -- at the time he was reinstated, activated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who are you speaking of now? What is the name --

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm speaking of Papric Miladin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll come back to this point on whether he was replaced a bit later on in your evidence. Now, whilst you were in your cell on the 26th of May, did you hear anything significant?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 26th of May, 1992 exactly at 8.00 I began hearing the shelling of the municipality of Sanski Most from heavy artillery weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, may I suggest you stop here and resume after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's a suitable moment to stop, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have a 30-minute break, resuming at just before 11.00. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, one matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I've spoken with Ms. Fauveau, and she's not ready to cross-examine today. I may actually finish, I think, before the end of the session today, but I'm perfectly happy for her to start tomorrow if that leaves her better prepared.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I can begin today, but I will not complete it. I have a part of the cross-examination for which I'm quite ready, and I think that will take up the rest of the time today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that's a practical way of dealing with it. Mr. Cayley, please, when we resume, do tell us the number -- exhibit number of --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's 798, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, before we begin, again I wanted to make a few comments about General Talic's comments about the diary, and simply about the order and presentation of evidence in this case. As you know, Rule 85 of the Rules of Procedure describes the order of evidence, and evidence is called in a common law fashion, evidence for the Prosecution, evidence for the Defence, Prosecution evidence and rebuttal and so on. In your guidelines that you yourself stated to us, on the 23rd of January of 2002 you in essence stated at page 672 that the accused wherever possible, you said, "It was desirable that the accused should give evidence before the evidence of any other witnesses." And you mention that in some cases this hadn't happened that, witness -- the accused had decided to give evidence at the end of the case. I would also mention to you Rule 90, which deals with the testimony of witnesses and within Rule 90(G) gives the Prosecution the right of cross-examination of any witness, including the accused, when statements like these are made. And what I would say is, whilst knowing that in civil law trials, accused are able to rise and make comments about the evidence, at that point in time General Talic was giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: He was making a comment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, if that is your assertion, I'm telling you to stop because the Trial Chamber does not consider what General Talic stated as part of his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. That makes me content.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm making it clear. I allowed General Talic to stand up first because I didn't know what kind of complaint, if -- complaint it was. Secondly, because respective of common law or civil law, whatever, if at any given moment the accused feels that his point of view is not being presented in accordance with his wishes or in accordance with his instructions or in accordance with his opinion, he has every right to point that out. He can ask to do it directly with counsel, asking for a break, or as happened earlier on today the way he did it, but don't take it that the Trial Chamber is considering his statement as part of his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That makes me content, because as you know, I'd like to cross-examine him on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Definitely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If he makes statements such as these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He has the right to give evidence or not to give evidence at the right stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Between now and then, if he has -- he or even Mr. Brdjanin -- I mean, I'm -- what I'm saying is not limited to General Talic. If any one of them want to rise and make a statement under the direction and control of the Trial Chamber -- and I want to make myself clear on this -- I will not allow a situation to arise whereby the accused will take over from the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm content, Your Honour. You've made it clear it's not evidence, so that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if that's the position for future comments, then I'm content.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely not evidence, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, before the break you had stated that you had heard the shelling of Sanski Most. Now, just to be absolutely clear about this, you didn't see the shelling take place because you were in a cell in the police station; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 641.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this is a document dated the 26th of May of 1992, Sanski Most Serbian municipality civilian protection municipal staff. And this is an order given pursuant to the conclusions of the Crisis Staff and the civilian protection staff. And the order is that the displaced population which withdrew from the Mahala, Muhici, and Otoke settlements to the Krkjevci is to be transferred by a Sana Trans DB socially owned enterprise bus to the sports hall for care and accommodation. Serbian Territorial Defence military police shall provide security for the column. Now, Mr. Karabeg, when if at all, did you find out that the displaced population from these areas had been moved to the sports hall in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were transferred on the 27th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's not the question I asked you. The question I asked you is: When did you personally find out that the population had been moved, bearing in mind that you were in a prison cell behind the police station. Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall it. I learnt about the transfer of the population -- I don't know whether it was the 27th or the 28th of May. During a visit by Tomo Delic and Nemanja Tripkovic and Boro Savanovic who came to visit us in the prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you learn about the transfer of the population during their visit to you?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: They visited us in the prison about 8.00 p.m. to treat us with some coffee and brandy, and they saw the smoke from the houses burning in Gornja Mahala, because Gornja Mahala is in the immediate vicinity on the other side of the Sana River and Tomo Delic informed us that their heroes, as he put it, had liberated Gornja Mahala and Otoke from extremists, that Gornja Mahala had been set on fire and that he had a videotape showing the burning of Gornja Mahala. And that his father had said that the Serbs would control Sanski Most for the next 500 years and that only -- not more than five Serbs would die; that from Krkojevci they had transferred the population, who had apparently fled their houses, and Krkojevci is right next to Gornja Mahala, 1 kilometre away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just remind the Court who were Tomo Delic, Nemanja Tripkovic, and Boro Savanovic.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Boro Savanovic and Nemanja Tripkovic were in the executive board of the SDS of Sanski Most, the highest body of the SDS party in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Tomo Delic?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: And Tomo Delic also. He was also a member. He came in uniform with the helmet on his head. At the time I didn't know, but he headed the Serbian defence forces in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 643.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the Mahala in late May of 1992, there were Muslims -- there were Muslim individuals who had weapons; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were not there at the time, but did you subsequently hear from anybody about the strength or otherwise of the resistance of those armed Muslims who were in the Mahala when it was attacked?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no resistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you hear that from?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard it from Tomo Delic himself, among others. He never mentioned any fighting in Mahala. He didn't say, "I have a video recording of the combat in Mahala" but he said, "I have a video recording of the burning of Mahala."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you read this exhibit in front of you. And the part that interests me are the first two paragraphs of the order. "The terrain in the area of Mahala --" and again, it's a conclusion pursuant to a decision of the Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality. And it states: "Order. The terrain in the area of Mahala, Otoke, and Muhici should be sanitized in order to carry out this out, the following shall be done. Bodies must urgently be recovered, identified, and buried in the designated place, a marked burial site." When did you discover that individuals had been killed in these three locations?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learnt it while I was in prison, because we had a young man who objected to all this, and when he was on duty he would tell us about what was going on in Sanski Most. And in October 1995, during the liberation of Sanski Most I was present when this grave site was unearthed and attended the burial and identification of the people killed in those days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Concentrating on May of 1992 for the moment, did you know at the time how many people had been killed in these places that are mentioned in this order?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you subsequently find out?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Subsequently I did find out. I couldn't in May because I was in the prison and I had no contact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people, if you can remember -- if you don't know, say you don't know. But how many people were killed in these three places as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Forty-two.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit -- if the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 646, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one last point. Where were those bodies buried pursuant to this order that's in front of you? Do you know? Again, if you don't know, just say you don't know. Do you know where the burial site was?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know where they were buried, because in 1995 I was present during the unearthing. It is Greda -- Greda in Sanski Most. The location is Greda, where a hole had been dug and the corpses thrown in.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, do you have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This, witness, is a regular combat report by General Talic. And the paragraph that interests me -- it refers to a number of matters concerning the 1st Krajina Corps at the time, but I just wish to read a couple of paragraphs from this particular report. In paragraph 1 in the seventh -- eighth line, it states the following: "There is still some weak resistance to confiscation of weapons in the wider area of Prijedor, Sanski Most, and Kljuc. The armed formations have been broken up, but some of their components from individuals to squads are still resisting the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as they flee. A large number of armed rebels have been captured in these towns." Now, Witness, when you were arrested in Sanski Most on the 25th of May of 1992 did you have a weapon with you?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether the mentally retarded man that was in the prison cell with you was armed when he was arrested?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any of the people that were in a cell with you armed when they were arrested? Do you know? If you don't know, simply say "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single person was armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 2: "The units of the 1st Krajina Corps are holding the positions taken earlier and the front line has not moved. Cooperation with the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina MUP in mopping up the terrain and confiscating weapons from illegal formations in the area of Prijedor, Sanski Most, and Kljuc continues." Mr. Karabeg, in May of 1992 at this time did you see the police and the army working together, as it states in this report, to the Main Staff of the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did I see it? I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was running the police station where you were? Who was running the prison cells where you were, the police or the army?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you. There were both the army and the police. In the compound, there were some army members as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether those army members were members of the local Territorial Defence or of the 6th Brigade? And again, if you don't know the answer to that question, simply say "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, because they wore all kinds of insignia. They even had three or four different insignia on their uniform. It was considered a kind of heroism.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that you saw in and around the prison that there were members of the military police. How did you know they were military policemen?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, until then and in those days we knew what the police uniforms were like and we also knew what the army uniforms were like, and we distinguished them by their uniforms because in those days the policemen did not wear camouflage uniforms. They all -- they were still wearing those old uniforms, the uniforms worn by the regular police while it existed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say that you saw members of the army, what colour uniforms were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them had these new camouflage uniforms, but quite a number of them were wearing those old SMB or olive/grey uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These are the uniforms that you were familiar with from the JNA, correct, the SMB?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. Those uniforms. Those are the ones I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What colour were the new camouflage uniforms, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several colours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the police, what colour uniforms were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police were still wearing those old uniforms made of blue cloth. But around the second half of July I started seeing policemen wearing camouflage uniforms as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Blue camouflage uniforms or green camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were blue camouflage uniforms. There were green camouflage uniforms. There was sort of a yellowish greenish camouflage uniforms. Those are the colours I can remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, there came a time, I think after the 29th of May of 1992 -- and I may have got the date wrong, so correct me if I have -- where you were asked to write a statement with Kurbegovic. Do you recall that time?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you asked to put into that statement?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was like this, you see: The people possessed arms. They had weapons in their possession, individuals, that they had purchased from Serb reservists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which people are you talking about? You're talking about the Muslim people?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "the people possessed arms," which people are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Individual Muslims and Croats. Which they had purchased from Serb reservists with a registration number on them. There was the number and the name to whom the weapon had been sold. And they insisted that I, Redzo, and Suad write a statement which would be broadcast on Radio Sana saying that the people should return those weapons. The same was done with Faik Biscevic, who was captured at Magarice by members of the army. And according to what he said and which was confirmed by others, a pistol was leant at his -- on his forehead. He was given a telephone receiver so that he should tell the people over Radio Sana that the people should return and surrender their weapons. So you see, they knew by name, each citizen -- a non-Serb citizen that owned a rifle, because he had purchased it from their reservists. And on this list the name was noted down as well as the number of the rifle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the transcript says "according to what he said and which was confirmed by others, a pistol was leant at his -- on his forehead." That must be a mistranslation. I have no idea what that means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Sir, could I ask you to explain this. We may -- it may just be and probably it is a mistake in the interpretation. What were you told by Faik Biscevic or others when he was -- relating to when he was asked or forced to pick up the telephone and make the appeal that has been -- that you have mentioned to the people over Radio Sana? What I want is the clarification from you as to how does a pistol fit in all this. Did someone put a pistol next to his temple, to his head, or what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I try to demonstrate it. It wasn't on his forehead but here to the side, to his temple.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You were told that someone put a pistol to his temple.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Faik was the first to tell me about it, who was brought to the prison in the night of the 28th of May from Magarice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the statement that you were forced to make, you did not personally make that statement on the radio. It was read out by somebody else; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We wrote it on a piece of paper. We signed it. Somebody took it to the radio station and read it there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear it yourself, the statement being read out, or not?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear it. We didn't have that possibility of listening to the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 656, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, this is an order, as you can see, of the Crisis Staff of the Sanski Most municipality, and it is an order given -- apparently an order adopted on the 30th of May of 1992. And the only paragraph that interests me in this particular order is the first one. "The director of the public utilities enterprise is ordered to provide machinery and manpower for the burial of persons killed in combat operations in Vrhpolje and Hrustovo." When did you find out that there had been combat operations in these two places? Bearing in mind again that you were in a prison cell behind the police station.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard it when I left for the Manjaca camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was in August of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Precisely on the 28th of August 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you hear had happened in Vrhpolje and Hrustovo?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that people had been killed, women, children, and old people. I heard that the -- in the Merdonovic family, 17 people had been killed, women, children, the old man Merdonovic, his four sons, who were otherwise working abroad in Switzerland.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you hear about this from?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard this from the camp inmates, the detainees who were in the camp there and who were originally from these areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you're referring to "the camp," you're referring to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I'm referring to the Manjaca camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they say who was responsible for these killings at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. Members of the military, of the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which army?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the army -- the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army, at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we can look at Prosecutor's Exhibit 657 very briefly. I just really want to draw Your Honours' attention to this document. I'm not going to ask the witness any questions. And if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Prosecutor's 657, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, which part of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
