utterances.text: Paragraph 3, line 5. And if Prosecutor's 661 could be made ready.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is again a regular combat report of the 1st Krajina Corps command to the Main Staff of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's dated 2nd June. "The wider area of Sanski Most, Prijedor, and Kljuc are under the control of our units. Mopping up of the area is underway." Now, if we can now refer to P661. Do you have 661 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this is a set of conclusions of the Crisis Staff, the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most, at a session held on the 4th of June, 1992. And it reads as follows: "1. Mirko Vrucinic, Nedeljko Rasula and Colonel Nedjo Anicic shall be in charge of resolving the issue of prisoners and their categorisation and deportation to Manjaca. First category, politicians. Second category, nationalist extremists. Third category, people unwelcome in Sanski Most municipality. In view of this, have a talk with Colonel Stevilovic from the 1st Krajina Corps." Now, Witness, whilst you were in prison at the police station did you ever hear talk of these categories of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you were to categorise yourself, which category would you place yourself in?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would place myself in the category of a non-Serb, because I'm not of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying, then, that the reason for your deportation was simply because you were a non-Serb?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I'm a Bosniak, a balija, or a Croat Ustasha.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that you appear on a list where you are categorised as an extremist? And we'll look at that list in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. I had seen no lists. I was arrested among the first. Maybe they had an opinion on me concerning this. And the first arrest began on the 25th of May, and I was arrested among the first. But in the prison I already found that retarded person, Meho, also known as Znojko, who is also a Bosniak, a balija just like I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 2 of this document -- and we'll get to the list in a moment. But in paragraph 2 of this document, it says: "The Crisis Staff hereby decides to appoint Drago Vujanic prison warden. Dismiss Papric." Now, you stated earlier in your evidence that when you arrived at the prison that Papric was in charge. Were you aware at any time that he was replaced by Drago Vujanic as the prison warden?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear about that, but I could assume so by the visits.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw Drago Vujanic at the police station; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, up until the 10th of June -- 9th, 10th of June of 1992, was there any violence against any of the prisoners at the police station cells, if you can recall? Up until that time.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to the 10th of June, we who were imprisoned, nobody even touched us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you say you were treated well until the 10th of June?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they didn't treat us badly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if I can just show you Prosecutor's Exhibit 663. And this is a document to the commander of the Manjaca military training facility command, and it is the last paragraph of this document which interests me. "We wish to let you know that we are still holding several persons in the detention rooms in the public security station and that we shall also send them to you for further procedure after the operative processing." A simple question: On the 6th of June of 1992, were you in the detention rooms of the public security station in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was, in prison, which is in the courtyard of the police station, the public security service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you can remember, how many other Muslims were with you at that time, on the 6th of June, at the public security station?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of those who I had listed; however, the number increased.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To how many approximately, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that there were 14 or 15 of us. In one of the cells, 7; and the other cell, I believe 8. However, in the meantime, Meho, the one I talked about, they let him go. That also -- Marinko -- Marinko had been set free, as well as Ibro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, it says at the beginning of this order that "In accordance with the agreement reached with the Banja Luka Corps command, Colonel Stevilovic and the chief of the police department of the Banja Luka security services centre, Stevan Markovic, we are sending you a group of persons who were captured during combat operations in the municipality of Sanski Most, as well as the persons who cooperated with them in the course of preparations for an armed uprising in the municipality of Sanski Most." Are you aware that on or about the 6th of June of 1992 there was a transfer of prisoners from Sanski Most to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that. It was the second group of prisoners from Sanski Most which were transferred to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, only if you can recall this matter, do you know what date this second group were transferred?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 3rd of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the date of this order is the 6th of June of 1992, so how is it possible that they were sent on the 3rd of June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do not know. I cannot tell you. However, the first group was transferred to Manjaca on the 3rd of June, approximately 152 individuals from the school of Hasan Kikic; and the second group, approximately 172 persons, on the 6th of June from the prison, from the Betonirka, and from the hall Dvorana [phoen] in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, again, bearing in mind that you were in a prison cell while this was taking place, when did you find out that these transfers had been made?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at -- to tell you -- I can tell you on the same day, because the people from the cells were transferred to the prison. Ibro Kuzelj was released, and he was already in Manjaca with the first group on the 3rd of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, I'm not -- I don't understand the answer to that question fully. Again, I'm asking you how did you know that these groups, these two groups, had been transferred from Sanski Most to Manjaca camp if you were in a prison cell behind the police station?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well individual persons from the cells were sent -- transferred to Manjaca. Concretely from the cell number 1, Stipe Catic, Saletovic Fikret, Ismet Jakupovic, Ismet Alagic were sent and transferred to Manjaca. They were called out, taken, and we immediately assumed, which turned out to be right, that they were sent and transferred to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you subsequently meet up with these people at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I met them there all, all of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I want to move to the period of the 9th or 10th of June of 1992, when I know conditions changed for you at the police station. Can you tell the Judges what happened around that time to you.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up till the 9th of June, I was in the prison. Once I was called for questioning by Dosenovic, who was carrying out the inquiry. With him I had -- I had a correct questioning session, even a pleasant one. He asked me about my past work, about the work of the executive board. He asked me questions. And on Christmas on the 24th and the 25th of December, 1991 I went to Croatia. That was one of the questions, why did I go? And I went, in fact, to Croatia because for the central heating for Sanski Most we ordered a big boiler from the TPK. And after that Christmas, the exchange rate changed between the dinar in Croatia and the rest of Yugoslavia. The exchange rate of dinar in Croatia was 1 to 2, compared to the rest of Yugoslavia. And so in order not to pay a double price for these -- this heating boiler, we went to Croatia to re-confirm that contract and to have this order re-confirmed. On the 9th of June, I was called out --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now we're talking about 1992 now.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm speaking of 1992. Yes, that was 1991, and now I am going back to 1992, on the 9th of June, 1992. At 10.30 I was called for what they call processing. Osmancevic Haso, Kurbegovic Redzo, and Faik Biscevic. We were interrogated separately, individually, each one in a separate room. The interrogation was carried on by Stanic Rajko, also known as Rajkica, who began by saying, "Do tell us what you had been doing. But first let me ask you a question: Do you know where Adil Draganovic is?" I answered, "No, I don't know." "But let me tell you. Adil Draganovic is in Manjaca. He wants to join a single nation -- party, and that is where he is now." This is the way we talked. Otherwise Rajkica and I, we were acquaintances. I asked them, "What do you want to know?" And he said, "You know, I want to hear what you want -- what I want to know." Then he left, and three persons who were here, they started beating me. They really beat me, and I concluded that the beating took an hour. And then Rajkica would tell me -- say again, "Tell me again." So we talked another three to five minutes. It wasn't like that. And then Rajkica left the room, and again they were beating me for about an hour's time. The third time he came in, he said -- he said, "Mirzo, write it down." And then I wrote Mirzo Karabeg from Sanski Most, member of the SDS. He said "No, Mirzo, this isn't it." So he left, and again they continued to beat me. But I was sitting on a chair, and they brought another chair through which I had to push my legs. Two were beating me on my head, my shoulders, my back, and the third one was beating me on my soles, the soles of my feet, and on my legs and with full force. After that, some -- an hour passed, and Rajkica returned. And he said, "Mirzo, get down. Go down and think it over." I went down to the ground floor. I went to the corner, sit down, look in the corner -- and raise -- I had to raise my head and look on the wall. I -- people were -- I don't know how the people heard. But anyway, they were still beating me with fists. Then I don't know from where, a cable. After that they took me back, and after all of this I asked whether I could drink a bit of water. They gave me a pitcher like this and I drank the water. Then a policeman came, and he said, "Take your things." I collected my belongings and from the prison went to the Betonirka facility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you stop there, because I have a few questions to ask you. Stanic, who was he?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stanic Rajko used to be a judge, the municipal judge in the municipal court in Sanski Most. And in that case, he was the investigator who was doing the interrogations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of the people that were beating you in the interrogation room?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were their names?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zoric. He's also an investigator in the police. I just can't remember his first name. Mico Krunic. And there was a third, younger man whose name I cannot recall but who was wearing -- and I saw that very well -- a very neat military uniform with Chetnik insignia, the cockade, and some other symbols indicating Serb-hood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of physical condition were you in prior to leaving for Betonirka?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was all beaten up. It is very hard to describe the condition I was in. I was in terrible condition. You see, it was the first time in my life to get a beating, the first time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said on the final occasion you went downstairs and that a number of people came off the streets to beat you. Who were these people?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I didn't dare turn around. I wasn't allowed to see them. But judging by the comments I heard, I heard that individuals came and asked, "Who is that?" I am not a hundred per cent sure, but I am 99 per cent sure that it is someone called Kudro, a neighbour of mine, who replied, "It's my neighbour, Mirzo." I didn't dare turn around to see who was beating me, because maybe if I had turned around that moment I wouldn't be sitting here today. I would have been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you beaten with when you were on the ground floor when you're at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: With fists, feet, pieces of electric cable, and wooden poles, wooden planks -- a pole, actually, as we call it in our jargon.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if you could hand these photographs out. This is P799, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you put that on the projector next to you, please, Mr. Karabeg. What is this place?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the garages of Betonirka.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And perhaps for the record, the witness is referring to Prosecutor's Exhibit 799.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whereabouts were you detained in this set of garages?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was detained in the third one. One, two, three, this one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the witness is indicating the red door of the garages on the left of the photograph, the end door on the left as one looks at the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I with your permission add, in those days these garages did not have this roof, and this part here was missing too. It was built after the war. So there were just these three garages, without any roof, with a flat concrete slab on top.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How big was the room that you were kept in at Betonirka, approximately? I mean, I suppose you --

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, approximately 3 metres by 6 metres. 3 metres wide, 6 metres long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until what point in time were you kept in this room?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the 7th of July, the 7th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many prisoners were kept in this cell with you? The least number and the most, if you can remember.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The least were there when I arrived. I found four people there. The largest number was 36.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at a point in time, there were 36 people in a room that was 6 by 3 metres; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the food that you received like? What was the quality of the food?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were given food in the morning and in the evening. Usually it was leftovers from their men who were working round the prison or the MUP. What was left over was distributed amongst us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the sanitary conditions like?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sanitary conditions were dreadful. We were shut up in this cell. We would be released in the morning for five to ten minutes and in the evening for five to ten minutes. We had to relieve ourselves in the garage, both to urinate and for our bowel movements. But when we were allowed outside, we could use the field toilet that was there within the compound of this camp. We slept on the concrete. We had nothing as a cover. Once we were given some styrofoam. But I think this was intentionally done because when you lie down on this foam, it breaks, it cracks and then you have to remove it because it hurts you. It's like pieces of stone or sand bothering you as you lie down, so you have to put it away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said earlier in your evidence that you'd been beaten before you arrived at Betonirka. What medical facilities were made available for the treatment of your injuries at Betonirka?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had none.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've said already there were 36 people in this room. How was the room ventilated? How did you get air in this room?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the side, there was a small window and that was all. But the problem was that people complained of -- especially in the central garage, there was no window at all, in the garage in the middle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your room, did you have sufficient air?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all. There was not sufficient air. There was 36 in that one room inside all day long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you manage to sleep with 36 people in one room?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. It was like this: Due to the mistreatment, the conditions, sometimes one falls asleep but they wouldn't let you fall asleep even then. There was a man called Milan Martic who was the worst. And when he was shift leader, he would designate one of us in the garage to watch so that all of us would remain standing all night. And as a reward, the person watching can sit down. We were loathe to accept, but if you didn't accept you would get beaten. And then every 15 minutes he would send a policeman in to check, to peep in and to check with a flashlight whether we were still on -- all on our feet. This went on like this from 7.00 in the evening, when his shift started, until 7.00 in the morning, when it ended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you understand was in the charge of the camp at Betonirka?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the main person in the camp was Vujanic Drago and his deputy Mico Krunic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of any of the guards?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall many names of guards, but just now for the moment the names don't come to me. But unfortunately these were all people I knew. These were all people from Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us talk about the physical violence at Betonirka. And if you can give a summary of what happened to you in that camp to the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the interrogation ended in the prison and the mistreatment there --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And here you're talking about the public security station now.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm talking about the 9th of June on -- 9th of June, 1992. A Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. guard told me, "Pick up your things and move to Betonirka." When I got there, I was told, "Go to garage number 3." I left my things there that same moment I was called out for beating. This man Martic started beating me immediately, and he was the first one to ask me, "What did you want to do to our children," he said. That was the first time I heard of it. And he beat me until 11.00 in the evening. That day, the 9th of June, I was beaten from 10.30 in the morning until 11.00 in the evening. I don't know whether there was perhaps a pause of two hours in between. If we were to add up all the pauses of five to ten minute, maybe they would amount to two hours. And the time it took for me to move from the prison to Betonirka, which is about a few hundred metres away, and it took me about 15 minutes to get there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when he was asking you about what you wanted to do to our children, what was referring to?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the radio, they started reporting that I had lists for circumcision of young boys of three and a half and for raping Serb girls. At first they said of six, eight, ten, twelve years of age, and they said that they had found those lists in my drawer. Afterwards I learnt -- because you know what people are like -- nobody asked themselves whether these lists really existed, but everyone said, "How could he have been so crazy as to keep those lists in his drawer?" So you can imagine the kind of propaganda they had. To preempt everything, they said that there were these lists that they had found in my drawer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you written these lists?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. It never occurred to me. Let me add, the last time I went into my office was on the 19th of April, 1992, and I was arrested on the 25th of May, 1992, which means that if there had been any lists, they would have been disclosed. No reasonable or intelligent man ever had any such ideas. But let me repeat, their propaganda was that they had found those lists in my drawer, and the people residence reaction was, "How could he have been so crazy as to have kept those lists in his drawer," lists that had never existed nor had the compiling of any such lists ever occurred to anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've talked about when Martic beat you. And now I want to move on to the time that you refer to when Martic and Kajtez beat you. Can you tell the Judges what happened on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: After, I think, about two days, Nihad Kljucinic was suspected of the same thing, who was with me in Betonirka but not in the same garage. About 7.00 in the evening we were allowed out, but Martic and Kajtez were beating Nihad. "Where are those lists," they said. After beating Nihad, they called me and they said to Nihad, "Here is your pal. You will find out from him where his lists are." They ordered me to kneel down like a donkey, on my -- go down on my hands and knees. They gave Nihad a stick to beat me with. As he started to beat me gently, they picked up the stick and continued beating him, swearing at him, and then hitting me a couple of times as well. After that, they let Nihad go and they continued beating me, the two of them, with these batons. And there was a car that Martic drove, and they pushed me against the car. Martic took a stick and put it under my chin. Kajtez took a knife as if to cut off my ear. Then they continued beating me. I don't know what kind of a system they had, but as I was between the two of them, one would -- would hit me with his behind and the other one would hit me with his stick and vice versa. They went on beating me like this for all of two hours. And you know what was typical? They beat me within the compound of Betonirka, and the people from Kruhari -- and this is a neighbourhood inhabited 99 per cent by Serbs -- behind the wire fence were watching this, and they were rooting as if they were watching a match, of course in their favour. "Beat him, the motherfucker. What did he want to do to our children," they were saying. "People like that should not be allowed to walk on this earth."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever told why you were being beaten?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you. Because of this list. I had a list. But did they find the list in my drawer? And they're beating me and demanding the list of me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I don't want to go through every beating up until the 7th of July, when you left Betonirka camp, but was there a day during the time that you were there when you were not beaten?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you. I believe that it might have been on the last and one but last day that I spent in Betonirka that I wasn't beaten, and that could have been the 6th and 7th of July, because around 11.00 when they had vacated Betonirka and sent everyone to Manjaca, there were six of us left from Betonirka that were sent on to prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever beaten by somebody called Tonci at Betonirka?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on the 7th of July of 1992, where were you moved to?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you're talking about the public security station in Sanski Most; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, the prison that I was in prior to Betonirka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in this building? What was the period of time that you remained here?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 7th of July until the 28th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how were you treated at the public security station during the period from the 7th of July until the 28th of August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the treatment was the same, but the beatings became rarer after representatives of the International Red Cross arrived and after we were registered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did the beatings become less regular after members of the International Red Cross arrived?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am unable to give you an answer, but all I could say is that that very moment when I was registered by the International Red Cross I started to live with a little more hope of survival, that I wouldn't be killed, because representatives of the International Red Cross after interviewing us -- when interviewing us would not allow anyone from the police to be present. We were alone with them, and with each one of us they conducted a frank and honest interview. They inquired about the conditions we were living in, our health, whether we had any contact with our families. And from then on, we were allowed every Saturday to meet with members of our family within the prison compound for 10 to 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the beating that you got on the 22nd of August of 1992 just before you left for Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe that beating.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was like this: When I said that they started beating us less frequently, they beat us on Saturday evening so that we could recover by next Saturday, when our family members came to visit us. On that 22nd of August, I remember very well it was a Saturday evening. We had been accustomed to this portion of beatings that we would get until next Saturday came. And five of us, we were in cell number 2 in the prison, myself, Osmancevic, Nihad Kljucinic, Osman Talic, and Franjo Ilicic. Just then we had been released to go and wash, to the toilet, and we went to the toilet to wash. We returned to the cell and one of the policemen asked our names. I said my name was Mirzet Karabeg, and everyone else gave his name. And when it came to Osmancevic's turn, he asked him, "Is that who you are?" And he started beating him. And he came back to the cell, and we asked why he beat him, and he said, "I don't know. He asked me my name, and he hit me about ten times. He kicked me and he hit me with his fists." We sat down in the cell. First Osman Talic was called out. We thought that Osman Talic was going to clean up his canteen and to be in the fresh air for a while at least. After --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, I think we better stop here for the time being, and the witness can have a rest too. And Mr. Karabeg, you will continue after the break, because we need to break now because we have certain standards that we have to keep. Thank you. Thirty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Cayley. As you see, we are just two of us now. Judge Janu is temporarily indisposed. She will hopefully be with us tomorrow. In the meantime, we are applying the special rule that we have and continuing with just the two of us here. Yes, Mr. Cayley. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honour, I want to state an objection to continuing with just two Judges. I just want to make it a matter of record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I join Mr. Ackerman in his objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Mr. Cayley, do you have to say anything about -- are you objecting too?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No. I'm not objecting, but I obviously have respect for the Defence's objection. I -- could you remind me of the rule, because I don't really have it to hand. I remember in a previous case in which this happened, we -- it was done under Rule 70(B) as a deposition. But I know after judge Riad's long illness that the rules were changed to allow continuation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are -- we're talking of Rule 15 bis. And there are three or four different scenarios, the first scenario being that under capital A, "If a Judge is, for illness or --" in this case, it is illness as you may have noticed in the course of -- Judge Janu wasn't feeling well yesterday, and she wasn't feeling well this morning, and she still isn't feeling well. "If a Judge is, for illness or other urgent personal reasons, or for reasons of authorised Tribunal business, unable to continue sitting in a part-heard case for a period which is likely to be of short duration, and the remaining Judges of the Chamber are satisfied that it is in the interests of justice to do so, those remaining Judges of the Chamber may order that the hearing of the case continue in the absence of that Judge for a period of not more than three days." The second option is under B, "If a Judge is, for illness or urgent personal reasons, or for reasons of authorised Tribunal business, unable to continue sitting in a part-heard case for a period which is likely to be of short duration, and the remaining Judges of the Chamber are not satisfied that it is in the interests of justice to order that the hearing of the case continue in the absence of that Judge, then those remaining Judges of the Chamber may nevertheless conduct those matters which they are satisfied it is in the interests of justice that they be disposed of notwithstanding the absence of that Judge, and the Presiding Judge may adjourn the proceedings." The third scenario I don't think I need to read because I do not have an indication that Judge Janu's illness is one which is expected to be longer than of a short duration. So I will -- you will spare me having to read that. Yes, that's the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you're making the order in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are -- we are applying, A -- 15 bis (A) -- applying A -- 15 bis (A). In other words, we are satisfied that it's in the interests of justice to continue hearing today in the absence of Judge Janu and then we'll take stock again of the situation tomorrow. But I have an indication from Judge Janu that tomorrow she will be here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, if I could remind you where we were prior to the break. And I would like to try and finish your evidence by quarter to 2.00. So we have 40 minutes left. You were explaining the 22nd of August, 1992. And a man by the name -- I think you said Osman Talic was called out. Can you briefly explain what happened to him and then explain very briefly what happened to you on that day.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said, Osman was called out. We thought he'd clear out the canteen and the yard, the yard of the police station and the prison. Some 40 minutes passed, and Osman returned to the cell, beaten up, holding his hand, and as he told us, one of the wardens took his hand and put it under a tap of -- turned on the hot water and we saw that from that hot water the skin and the tissue was scorched to the bone. After that, Nihad was called, Franjo, also beaten up. After that, I was called out. From the cell to the yard, it's some 20 metres, and I was escorted by a policeman, and two persons were talking among themselves. I came closer to them. I expected that they would be hitting me. One kicked me. He hit me, and then one of them said, "Look at Alija's warrior. Let me see if Alija taught you how to pray and to kneel." So I did kneel. I also placed my hands forward. I didn't see it, but he held in his hand a wooden leg of a table. He hit me like this. As I was kneeling, the second one in boots, he kicked me and said, "Get up. Your balija's mother. Bend again, kneel again, you balija." And they hit me again. But it was the other side of my shoulders. And so this lasted some 40 minutes. They took me back to my cell. I thought that I wouldn't survive that night and that I would die due to the pain. I sat out the whole night. We were, all of us, beaten up and in the morning when I got up, I then tried to lie down on my belly, on my stomach. I lay down, and in the morning when they let me go out to relieve myself and to wash up, I looked at myself in the mirror. On my back, the capillaries were like if you took a red marker and just drew some lines. And so for the next 20 days I was sleeping on my stomach. There was no chance of sleeping on my back or sideways. After 20 days, I could sleep for a time on my back but not on the sides. Neither on the left side nor on the right side, so that I had quite a few problems in sleeping. I had pains for about half a year. And even today I wake up in pain when I turn on my left side -- to sleep on my left side. Another characteristic aspect: One of them -- a person I didn't know -- he was a military officer, and another one, a policeman. His surname was Mauda but I don't know his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you say one of these individuals kicked you with his boot. Where did he kick you?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right here -- on the face and my head. As I was bending down. But don't think -- when the doors opened, I always took off first my glasses because they would certainly also break the glasses. I had a warden, in fact, who entered a cell at the Betonirka. He found my glasses. He took off my glasses and broke them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dane Kajtez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What injuries did you suffer as a result of being kicked in the face and the head?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a single tooth. I have artificial prosthesis. And if need be, I can show that but only to the Judges.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I think the Judges are satisfied that you've had your teeth kicked out of your head. On the 28th of August, you moved to Manjaca; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody that was with you at the police station remain at the police station?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were a group of 15 in the cells in the prison. Thirteen of us were taken out, and we were told to get on the bus and to remain. Kamber Hasib and Seferovic Emir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the two individual that is you've name right hand the two individuals that remained at the police station prison; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to them, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who by?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know who killed them, but I do know that they were killed. Their places -- they were disinterred, and then they were officially buried. And I was there when the exhumation took place and I saw them dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You arrived at Manjaca camp. What was the first thing that happened to you when you arrived at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would only like to make a comment. I believe that also among the Serbian nation there were also people with common sense and fine people. One of the wardens who escorted us -- and there were four of them -- when entering the bus, he said, "Sit in the bus and sit wherever you wish to sit on the bus."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're talking now about the trip from Sanski Most to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from Sanski Most to Manjaca. "You will be taken to Manjaca. I'm escorting you. Nobody is allowed to say anything bad against you and nobody dare touch you." And that is how it was, until we arrived to Manjaca. When we arrived to Manjaca, there were 49 of us on the bus: 13 from the police prison and the rest from the hall Krings. And when we arrived to Manjaca, we were -- we went off the bus, and they told us that there was another bus which will be taking the released detainees from Manjaca. And that's true. Because Klucinic Nihad came to Manjaca. And his father, who was 70 years, was leaving Manjaca. They didn't allow them to establish contact. They just waved to each other, waved hands. When we came to Manjaca, we were told that we would be going for a medical check-up in groups of eight. The eight of us in that group in which I was also, we had to undress completely. And two doctors, two physicians, who were also detainees from Sanski Most, were checking us, asking for our names, surname, place of birth, date of birth, and whether we have any injuries. And behind them, the guards of Manjaca, Serbs, were checking our belongings to see whether we have any money, any gold, or anything of any valuables among these objects that we brought in. After that, we dressed. After they checked our belongings and after they collected what was of value, they took us to a place where we then waited. After everybody has been examined, we were taken to the Manjaca camp, camp number 2. There was one camp but which was then divided into two with wire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, if you could stop there for a moment. And I just want to ask you a couple of questions. You said that the guards of Manjaca were checking your belongings to see whether you had any money, any gold, or anything valuable. Now, you also went on to say, "They collected what was of value." Why were they collecting these items? What for?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to appropriate these objects. Well, it was something which they wanted to take for themselves, their loot, because these things they took we've never seen them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall if you personally had anything taken from you?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I succeeded in hiding a valuable watch. It was a momento and it was a Tissot watch. I've never seen it again. I didn't have any money, and I had no other valuables, because they were already collected in Sanski Most in the prison and in the Betonirka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this watch that you had was taken from you at Manjaca by the camp guards; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd just like to show you a series of photographs which you haven't seen before and just to see if you recognise any of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These are some digital photographs that have been taken. If you could put it on the ELMO. And if you could take the map off, Mr. Karabeg. Sorry to ... Do you recognise these photographs?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell the judges what it is.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the barns where we were housed in Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, again -- and only if you remember -- do you recall which barn you were housed in? Is it one of the three that's portrayed in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me put it this way: As I told you, there were two parts of the camp. I was in camp 2, in the barn number 2. And if this is it, then it would be the central barn in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So the witness is indicating on this photograph that he believes that if this is camp number 2, then he was in the barn portrayed in the middle of this photograph. What is the exhibit number for this?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: 800. And this is Prosecutor's Exhibit 800. If I could show to the witness the next photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this is the interior of one of the barns. And they were all the same. Can you indicate in this photograph -- as I say, it may not be the barn that you were located in, but can you indicate on this photograph the area that you occupied whilst you were a prisoner at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first the door where one enters is here. And I was on the left very close there to the upper part at the beginning, and that is where I stayed and I slept also.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So the witness is indicating on this photograph of a barn on the -- at the end on the left by the door in the centre of the photograph. And that is Prosecutor's Exhibit 801.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when you arrived at Manjaca at the end of August of 1992, how would you describe conditions there?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: First when I came to Manjaca, what I observed was that there were many people who were just bones, skin and bones, very thin. And there were certain individuals who couldn't stand on their legs. And those very thin would then be picked up by two people -- they'd make like a seat with their hands and carry these very thin people. As far as the conditions are concerned, when you -- let me tell you. When you sleep on a concrete floor and you have nothing to cover yourself with, when you don't have sanitary conditions to maintain your personal hygiene, when you cannot -- there's no place to relieve oneself, where you're followed your every step and you have to be careful not to make a move which wouldn't please them, you cannot describe it otherwise as terrible conditions. When individuals are being beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there violence that you were aware of at Manjaca at the end of August and onwards until the time that you left?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the physical violence that you were aware of that was taking place in the camp during this time.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, it was like this: A detainee was beaten twice because he spoke to his brother across the wire fence. There was Begisba [phoen], a detainee who slept close to me went with a group of other detainees under escort to fetch water, to bring it back in a jerrycan, and he tried to pour clean water into the can and a guard approached him and beat him up because of this, and I saw him covered in blood. His name was Semin Vajzovic. And people continued to be taken for interrogation and to isolation cells for beatings. A group was brought in, I believe, of some 126 people from Kotor Varos and almost all of them were beaten. And we continued to hear screams during the night from the beatings in the isolation cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you personally the victim of any physical violence at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once a guard hit -- kicked me in the back because I was going to collect rain water in my can near the canteen where this was possible. I didn't see, as it was raining and I had a hood on my head, and he approached me from behind, kicked me, so I fell into the mud. And he said, "Get lost from there," and he swore at Alija -- Alija's mother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you know the names of any of the guards at Manjaca that were dishing out these beatings to the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I knew them by their nicknames. There was one called -- they called Spaga, another one they called Tito. And while I was at Manjaca, I avoided moving around very much. I tried to move as little as possible so as to emerge alive and well from there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak whilst you were at Manjaca to prisoners who had been there since June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they describe what conditions were like then?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were conditions in June of 1992 at Manjaca? Better than in August, worse than in August?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me put it this way: In June 1992 the people who arrived there first suffered some horrors. First of all, they were starved. Secondly, they had to do work duty. They were frequently beaten, especially cries could be heard from the isolation cell at night. And they called this interrogations. Furthermore, they frequently were subjected to a kind of call-out. They would take out all the detainees from all three stables. They would call out their first and last names. And then the other guards would enter the stables and search around to see if they could find anything of value to appropriate for themselves. I also attended such a call-out when I arrived at Manjaca. It was sometime the second or third day. So it could have been the 29th or the 30th of August when this happened. Food was given to them in the morning and in the evening, a small slice of bread.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did conditions improve between June and August of 1992, as far as you're aware, from your conversations with the inmates?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was like this: Talking to fellow inmates, they all said, and I felt it myself, that changes had occurred with the arrival of the International Red Cross. First of all, to start with the food. It was a great thing then to get a quarter of a loaf of bread in the morning and another quarter in the evening. The International Red Cross also conducted medical examinations. I had a case when a detainee Omer Kalic had some medical problems, and he asked me to talk to a young lady who was the interpreter there, to ask her if he could see a doctor who spoke German and he too spoke German. And he asked that with a group of patients who were being prepared for treatment in London that he be one of that group. And when the doctor examined him, he put him on that list. But that was the only way he could go. He had no other chances, because he had reported that he had this drainage tube fitted and his health problems, but they did not agree to have him examined, so this was one way in which the International Red Cross helped us. And it was mostly thanks to the International Red Cross that we survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 668.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You have five more minutes, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I see, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: 668, yes. And if you could hand it to me and I'll -- all right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, here in front of you, you see a list.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if that list could be placed in English on the ELMO, please. Actually, it's the other English list. They're the same, but they're numbered slightly different. Just so we have the same as the witness. Excuse me, Mr. President. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this is a list entitled "List of the most radical extremists in the area of Sanski Most." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is number 50 on this list?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Karabeg Mirzet, me. That's me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you go through this list and indicate whether or not these individuals ended up at the Manjaca camp, as far as you know. If you don't know, just say "I don't know." So just go through 1 to 50 and identify whether those people were at Manjaca camp.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me see. Talic Elhad, Malovcic Fikret - I'm just reading the names of the people with whom I was in the camp - Burnic Ferid, Sahmovic Eniz, Hodzic Rahim, Kamber Dzevad, Avdic Ismet, Handanagic Vahid, Karabeg Rasim, Smajlovic Ferid, Makic Husein, Supuk Bajro, Supuk Senad, Lovric Zdravko, Hromalic Mujo, Bahtic Rifet, Islamcevic Hakija, Celic Emsud, Kugic Senad, Omic Mehmed, Halilovic Nijaz, Sarcevic Fehim, Skripic Andjelko, Kolakovic Ismet, Marijan Josip, Krupic Omer, Besic Enver, Halimovic - not Halilovic - Midho, Sarajlic Salahudin, Zukic Esef, Krupic Ismet, Kuzelj Ibrahim, Maric Jakov, Lovic Sefik, Kamic Mirzet, Pasic Ibrahim, Zukic Asim, Karabegovic Samir, Kurbegovic Nedzo, Biscevic Fajko, Osmancevic Hase, Kljucinic Nihad, Talic Osman, Burnic Semso, Kicin Jusuf, Okcic Nesib, Karic Remzo, Sahic Suad, Karabeg Mirzet. I know all of them. They were all there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were all at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all at Manjaca, all of them. They were all from Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you describe these people as radical extremists?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: These people, their only fault is that they were not Serbs, that they were Bosniaks -- of Bosniak and Croat ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've now completed my examination-in-chief and I can offer the witness for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] That will be tomorrow, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I thank you, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. I thank you, Mr. Cayley. Cross-examination will commence tomorrow. I assume that Madam Fauveau will be starting. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will begin, and I'll certainly be using most of tomorrow's hearing time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Mr. Karabeg, we are stopping here for today. We will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00. And tomorrow you're going to face the first of the two cross-examinations that will take place. It will be the Defence team for General Talic that will cross-examine. I thank you once more, and you will now be escorted out of -- outside this courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We'll meet tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
